title: What is Flink's broadcast state pattern — a small, slowly-changing dataset (e.g., rules, config) is broadcast to all parallel instances of an operator via BroadcastStream, stored in BroadcastState, and used to enrich or control the processing of the main stream?
shortTitle: What is Flink's broadcast state pattern

s1_definition.profdef: The broadcast state pattern in Flink distributes a small, slowly-changing dataset to every parallel instance of a downstream operator so that each instance holds an identical copy in a special operator state called BroadcastState. You create it by marking a stream as broadcast with a MapStateDescriptor, connecting it to the main keyed or non-keyed stream, and processing both in a BroadcastProcessFunction or KeyedBroadcastProcessFunction. The broadcast side updates the shared state in processBroadcastElement, while the main side reads that state read-only in processElement to enrich, filter, or control each record, which is ideal for dynamic rules, feature flags, or reference configuration that must reach all partitions consistently.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has many fraud-checking clerks working in parallel, each handling a slice of the transaction stream. The bank's risk committee occasionally publishes an updated rulebook, for example "flag any transaction over five lakh rupees" or "block merchant category 7995." The broadcast state pattern is like photocopying that rulebook and placing an identical copy on every clerk's desk the moment it changes, so that no matter which clerk handles a given transaction, they all apply the same current rules. The clerks never edit the shared rulebook while processing transactions; they only read it. A dedicated rulebook channel updates every desk's copy whenever the committee changes the rules.
s1_definition.oneliner: Broadcast state replicates a small, slowly-changing rules or config dataset to every parallel operator instance, where the main stream reads it to drive its processing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The broadcast state pattern in Flink distributes a small, slowly-changing dataset to every parallel instance of a downstream operator so that each instance holds an identical copy in a special operator state called BroadcastState. You create it by marking a stream as broadcast with a MapStateDescriptor, connecting it to the main keyed or non-keyed stream, and processing both in a BroadcastProcessFunction or KeyedBroadcastProcessFunction. The broadcast side updates the shared state in processBroadcastElement, while the main side reads that state read-only in processElement to enrich, filter, or control each record, which is ideal for dynamic rules, feature flags, or reference configuration that must reach all partitions consistently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has many fraud-checking clerks working in parallel, each handling a slice of the transaction stream. The bank's risk committee occasionally publishes an updated rulebook, for example "flag any transaction over five lakh rupees" or "block merchant category 7995." The broadcast state pattern is like photocopying that rulebook and placing an identical copy on every clerk's desk the moment it changes, so that no matter which clerk handles a given transaction, they all apply the same current rules. The clerks never edit the shared rulebook while processing transactions; they only read it. A dedicated rulebook channel updates every desk's copy whenever the committee changes the rules.

**One line to remember:** Broadcast state replicates a small, slowly-changing rules or config dataset to every parallel operator instance, where the main stream reads it to drive its processing.

sections.s2_technical:
You begin by describing the broadcast state with a `MapStateDescriptor`, for example `new MapStateDescriptor<>("rules", String.class, Rule.class)`. You take the control stream, such as a stream of rule updates, and call `ruleStream.broadcast(descriptor)` to produce a `BroadcastStream`. Broadcasting means every parallel instance of the downstream operator will receive every rule-update record, as opposed to a keyed or round-robin partition where each instance sees only a slice. You then connect the main data stream to the broadcast stream with `mainStream.connect(broadcastStream)` and process it with a `BroadcastProcessFunction` for non-keyed main streams or a `KeyedBroadcastProcessFunction` for keyed main streams.

The process function has two methods. `processBroadcastElement` is called for each record on the broadcast side and is the only place allowed to modify the broadcast state; here you update the shared rules, for example `ctx.getBroadcastState(descriptor).put(rule.getId(), rule)`. Because Flink delivers broadcast records to every instance, each instance applies the same update, keeping the copies consistent. `processElement` is called for each record on the main side and gets read-only access to the broadcast state via `ctx.getBroadcastState(descriptor)`; here you read the current rules and apply them to the record, for example checking whether a transaction violates any active rule. The read-only restriction on the main side is deliberate and important: if each instance could mutate the state based on its own partition's data, the copies would diverge and the pattern would break.

Several senior nuances matter. The broadcast dataset must be small, because it is fully replicated to every instance and held in memory, so it suits rules, thresholds, feature flags, small reference tables, and configuration, not large datasets. Broadcast state is operator state with the UnionListState-like property that on restore each instance receives the full state, which fits its replicated nature. There is no ordering guarantee between the broadcast updates and the main records across instances, so you should design rules to be safe to apply slightly before or after a given main record, and if you need strict coordination you handle it explicitly. The pattern shines for dynamic behavior without redeploying: the risk team pushes a new rule onto the control topic and every instance picks it up live. It is the standard Flink answer to "how do I change business rules in a running stream job without restarting it."
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a fraud-screening job across many parallel instances, each handling a partition of the transaction stream keyed by account. The risk team needs to change fraud rules, such as the maximum allowed single-transaction amount or a blocked merchant list, at any time, and every instance must apply the new rules immediately and identically without restarting the job. This is exactly the broadcast state pattern: the rules are broadcast to all instances and stored in broadcast state.

Problem 2 — While rules change occasionally, transactions flow constantly, and each transaction must be screened against the current rules regardless of which instance processes it. The main stream must read the shared rules read-only and flag or pass each transaction. This is exactly the connected main-stream processing where processElement reads the broadcast state to control each transaction.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that reproduces the pattern. We define a `Rule` with an id, a type, and a threshold or value, and a `Txn` transaction. A `BroadcastRuleState` stands in for BroadcastState, holding the current rules, with an update method representing processBroadcastElement that every instance applies, and a read-only screen method representing processElement that checks a transaction against all active rules. A `ParallelInstance` wraps a copy of the broadcast state to show that multiple instances each hold an identical replica updated by the same broadcast records. A `BroadcastStateDemo` main class creates several instances, broadcasts a rule update to all of them, screens transactions on different instances to show consistent flagging, then broadcasts a changed rule and shows every instance immediately applying the new rule.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  broadcast:
    rules-topic: nbi.fraud.rules      # control/broadcast stream
    txns-topic: nbi.transactions      # main stream
    parallelism: 4                    # instances all get every rule
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four parallel instances, two broadcast rule updates, and four transactions screened on various instances.

Step 1: The first rule, flag any transaction over five lakh rupees, is broadcast. Every one of the four instances receives this identical rule and stores it in its broadcast state replica, so all four now hold exactly one rule. This is the broadcast delivery that keeps the copies consistent.

Step 2: A transaction of six lakh rupees for Rajesh is screened on instance zero. Instance zero reads its rule replica, sees the max-amount rule, and because six lakh exceeds five lakh, flags the transaction. The verdict comes from the shared rule regardless of which instance handled it.

Step 3: A transaction of two and a half lakh for Priya is screened on instance two. Instance two reads the same rule, sees that the amount is under five lakh, and passes it. Instances zero and two produced consistent decisions because they hold identical rules.

Step 4: The risk team pushes a second rule, block merchant CASINO7995, onto the control stream. It is broadcast to all four instances, each of which applies it, so every instance now holds two rules, again identically and without restarting the job.

Step 5: A small one-thousand-rupee transaction for Rajesh at merchant CASINO7995 is screened on instance one. Even though the amount is tiny, instance one reads the new block-merchant rule and blocks the transaction, proving the rule update took effect immediately.

Step 6: A three-lakh transaction for Priya at CASINO7995 is screened on instance three. Instance three also holds the new rule and blocks it. The demo shows that a single broadcast rule change was applied consistently across all instances live, which is the whole point of the pattern.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The broadcast state pattern in Flink is how you distribute a small, slowly-changing dataset to every parallel instance of an operator so they all hold an identical copy and apply it consistently. You describe the shared state with a MapStateDescriptor, mark your control stream as broadcast with that descriptor to get a BroadcastStream, connect it to your main stream, and process both in a BroadcastProcessFunction or, if the main stream is keyed, a KeyedBroadcastProcessFunction. The crucial detail is the split of responsibilities between the two methods. processBroadcastElement handles each record on the control side and is the only place allowed to modify the broadcast state, and because Flink delivers every broadcast record to every instance, each instance applies the same update and the copies stay consistent. processElement handles each record on the main side with read-only access to the broadcast state, reading the current rules or config to enrich, filter, or control that record. The read-only restriction on the main side is deliberate, because if each instance could mutate the state from its own partition the copies would diverge and the whole pattern would break.

There are important constraints and strengths. The broadcast dataset must be small, because it is fully replicated into memory on every instance, so it suits rules, thresholds, feature flags, small reference tables, and configuration, not large data. Broadcast state is a form of operator state that, on restore, gives every instance the full state, which matches its replicated nature. There is no strict ordering guarantee between broadcast updates and main records across instances, so you design rules to be safe applied slightly before or after a given record. The headline benefit is dynamic behavior without redeploying: a team pushes a new rule onto the control topic and every instance picks it up live, which is the standard answer to changing business logic in a running stream job without a restart.

At the National Bank of India this was the heart of our fraud-screening job. Transactions flowed keyed by account across many parallel instances, and the risk team maintained a control stream of fraud rules such as a maximum single-transaction amount and a blocked-merchant list. We broadcast those rules so every instance held an identical rule set in broadcast state, updated it only in processBroadcastElement, and in processElement each instance read the rules read-only to flag or block each transaction. The payoff was that when the risk team needed to react to a new fraud pattern, they pushed one rule onto the control topic and every instance applied it immediately, with no job restart and no inconsistency between partitions. I could demonstrate it concretely: screen a transaction before a rule existed and it passed, broadcast a block-merchant rule, and then the very next transaction to that merchant on any instance was blocked. Being able to explain the broadcast-and-connect mechanics, the read-write versus read-only split between the two methods, the small-dataset constraint, and the live-rule-update benefit is exactly what shows mastery of this pattern.
